verdict: DEFER (no NEW page; no ENRICH recommended as primary action). Reason: the queue description is wrong about the content. The paper does NOT empirically compare contractor returns or government take across regimes. It is a qualitative document analysis of 20 legal/regulatory/technical sources plus a stylised 100-unit cash-flow illustration that the authors say is 'not jurisdiction-specific', is 'not used to rank jurisdictions', and omits discounting; it reports no IRR, NPV or government-take percentage for the UK, Norway, Ghana or Nigeria, no sample of projects, and no estimate of resource-rent share. The one genuinely rent-relevant, citable material is (a) the royalty-versus-profit-tax mechanism (royalty fixed at 10 units while concession profit tax falls 18 to 8 as costs rise 45 to 70), which is textbook IMF/Tordo material the paper itself cites, and (b) the UK and Norway both at a 78% headline marginal rate on upstream profits, which makes the paper's point that identical headline rates hide different deduction, loss and administration rules. Neither justifies a research page; the better route is to cite the Tier 1 primaries (IMF 2012 'Fiscal Regimes for Extractive Industries'; Tordo 2007, World Bank WP 123; HMRC; Norwegian Tax Administration) directly. BACKLOG lead: [FIND] IMF (2012) Fiscal Regimes for Extractive Industries: Design and Implementation (doi 10.5089/9781498340069.007) and Tordo (2007) World Bank WP 123 as the Tier 1 anchors for a royalty-vs-rent-tax paragraph in concepts/resource-rents.md. OPTIONAL low-value ENRICH if T1 wants something now (T1's call; I do not recommend it): places/norway.md, section 'Caveats', after the bullet ending 'rather than spent down.[1]' add one sentence that the UK also carries a 78% headline marginal rate on upstream profits from 1 Nov 2024 (RFCT 30% + SC 10% + EPL 38%, EPL scheduled to end 31 Mar 2030) so the headline rate alone does not distinguish regimes; cite HMRC primaries, not Benin et al., for the rates. HOUSEKEEPING FINDING (independent of this paper, worth a separate fix): places/norway.md line 30 says 'the ordinary 22% company tax plus a 71.8% special petroleum tax'. The Norwegian primary says the 71.8% special rate is applied to a base net of the ordinary tax paid, so the two do not add to 78% (22% + 56% effective = 78%; 56% is the pre-2022 special rate, also the figure used on research/nassios-australia-lng-prrt-structural-limits.md). The sentence should say the combined marginal rate is 78%, with a 71.8% technical special-tax rate applied after deducting the ordinary tax.
claim_grade: Paper: C/D-claim on rent capture as such (qualitative mechanism argument and an illustrative model, not an estimate; the authors disclaim causal and ranking inferences). Factual descriptions of statutory rates in the paper (UK 30/10/38, Norway 78%) are A-claims only once confirmed against the primaries: Norway CONFIRMED against norskpetroleum.no (saved); UK RFCT 30% CONFIRMED against GOV.UK (saved); UK SC 10% and EPL 38% NOT independently confirmed. EDITORIAL 4c tier: peer-reviewed article in an established Elsevier journal (EIS is a CWTS-core, ANVUR class A title per OpenAlex) = source-quality level 2, but the four authors (University of the West of Scotland, Xi'an Fanyi University, Ravensbourne) have no established body of work on petroleum fiscal design visible in the paper's own reference list, are not in sources/audit/people-tiers.json, and the paper has 0 citations. Judged by the rubric: usable as a peer-reviewed synthesis of what the cited primaries say, not as 'prominent authority' social proof. Cite the Tier 1 anchors it rests on.

uncertainties: PARCEL IDENTIFICATION is by reproduction, not by the post: Puzycki does not name the parking lot or give parcel IDs. Waterline = 98 Red River St (prop 860621) is certain. The lot = prop 191605 (604 Driskill, Waller Creek Block 190 LLC) because it reproduces BOTH of the post's per-acre numbers ($175,042 vs $175k) and its 650/610 land-value ratio (1.067 vs 1.066) when the Waterline reproduces $1.08M at the same rate; this is a strong fit but I did not verify that the lot is physically 'across the street' from the tower. Say 'a parking lot in the same district', not 'across the street', unless T1 confirms on a map.

The post's rate is not the adopted rate: it is the FY2026-27 no-new-revenue rate $0.535466 (an unstated modelling choice that matches 'revenue-neutral'). 'Will pay' therefore overstates precision; at the adopted $0.579948 the figures are about $1.17M and $190k per acre. Also the city share only (footnote 2), and TCAD values are Jan-1-2026 certified (July 2026), unchanged in the Oct supplement.

The $650k/$610k pure-LVT numbers are a per-acre average (equal weighting of the two parcels, 3.07 vs 1.40 acres); acreage-weighted they would be about $814k/$764k. Do not quote them as the pair's revenue-neutral LVT bills. The qualitative point (near-equal bills) holds either way. Also: the Waterline value is mostly improvements ($513.6M of $620.6M), so any LVT bill would depend on how TCAD's land value is assessed; TCAD assigns block-wide per-acre land values ($34.85M/ac at the tower, $32.67M/ac on the lot, Original City blocks showing repeated rates such as $21.8M/ac), i.e. land values are mass-appraised, which is itself relevant to the 'land cannot be assessed' objection.

Prop Q official numbers: not reached. Election-night counts differ between two Community Impact timestamps (109,262/62,882 vs 109,375/62,952; Axios cited 109,011/62,719, page blocked). Cite as 'more than 63% against' and say unofficial, or fetch the Travis County canvass (Clarity ENR) later.

'3,650 acres / $4.4B' (CLE) and '15% of Downtown Austin' (Parking Reform Network) are UNVERIFIED. They should not appear on a wiki page unless a CLE or PRN document is found; if used at all, attribute to Puzycki as relaying CLE.

Texas Tax Code text is from texas.public.law (non-official mirror, 'updated May 26, 2025'); the official statutes.capitol.texas.gov site is a JavaScript shell from this network. The 2025 session may have amended s.26.04 (T1 should check whether the 1.035 multiplier and the 8% special-unit multiplier are still current; the City of Austin's FY2027 budget table shows 3.5% in the FY2027 row, which corroborates that the 3.5% was still operative for the 2026 tax year). Austin's 'unused increment rate' mechanism (the budget's rate table) means the cap is not strictly 3.5% per year in every year.

The wiki should not say 'a constitutional amendment would be required' on Puzycki's say-so. Supported by primaries: Art. VIII s.1(a)-(b) and Tax Code s.26.02 and s.23.01 put all property on one proportional basis; the 1915 Baker v. City of Houston ruling (already on the wiki) applied the earlier constitutional clause to a land-favouring split. Not located: any current legal opinion or CLE legality analysis for Texas, or whether a building-exemption design (the Washington State workaround) would survive. Hedge accordingly: 'the constitution requires property to be taxed in proportion to its value; the Houston Plan was struck down under that clause in 1915; whether a modern split-rate or building-exemption design is permissible has not been tested'.

Post characterisations not verified in primaries: that 'some of those same groups who opposed Proposition Q' back Prop I (Fox 7/CBS describe Prop I as a citizen-petition measure by Save Austin Now; the group link is the post's); 'a million-dollar logo boondoggle'; that new construction adds 'about half as much value' (Community Impact: $2.8B vs nearly $5.5B at peak two years ago, which supports it); 'roughly $100 million in planned spending' pared back (Community Impact: $109.5M of lost Prop Q revenue). The parks and library bond amount ($295M) and the 3 Nov 2026 date are in the post only; the city ballot form was not read.

The CLE evidence the post relays (Pittsburgh +13%, Pennsylvania +12% establishments) is CLE restating Oates-Schwab-type and Hanson (2022) results; the wiki's Tier 1 anchors for those are research/oates-schwab-pittsburgh.md and research/bourassa-pittsburgh-lvt-housing.md. Link there rather than citing the post or CLE for them.

EDITORIAL 4b and 4c for any page: Puzycki goes in a labelled 'Current debate' / 'Origin of the comparison' paragraph with his status stated ('an Austin zoning and platting commissioner and Strong Towns contributor who writes the City of Yes newsletter'); the numbers cited as support are the TCAD and city-budget records; no process narration ('reproduced this session'): say 'the comparison can be reproduced from the appraisal district's certified export'.
